title: I Hear from Heaven To-day
origin: Slave Songs of the United States (1867), No. 3, page 2; Port Royal Islands, South Carolina, collected by C. P. Ware.
note: Source verified directly against the Internet Archive's full-text scan of the original 1867 edition (item explicitly marked 'Not in copyright' by the Library). Page and collector credited exactly as printed in the book's own table of contents.
verses:
Hurry on, my weary soul,
And I hear from heaven to-day,
Hurry on, my weary soul,
And I hear from heaven to-day.

My sin is forgiven and my soul set free,
And I hear from heaven to-day.

A baby born in Bethlehem,
And I hear, etc.
De trumpet sound in de oder bright land.
My name is called and I must go.
De bell is a-ringin' in de oder bright world.

title: Praise, Member
origin: Slave Songs of the United States (1867), No. 5, page 4; Port Royal Islands, South Carolina, collected by C. P. Ware.
note: Source verified directly against the Internet Archive's full-text scan of the original 1867 edition. The book's own introduction notes this hymn's words closely match an older piece called 'Choral Hymns,' suggesting a shared older root.
verses:
Praise, member, praise God,
I praise my Lord until I die;
Praise, member, praise God,
And reach de heavenly home.

O Jordan's bank is a good old bank,
And I hain't but one more river to cross;
I want some valiant soldier
To help me bear the cross.

O soldier's fight is a good old fight,
And I hain't, etc.
O I look to de East, and I look to de West.
O I wheel to de right, and I wheel to de left.

title: The Lonesome Valley
origin: Slave Songs of the United States (1867), No. 7, page 5; Port Royal Islands, South Carolina, collected by C. P. Ware.
note: Source verified directly against the Internet Archive's full-text scan of the original 1867 edition. The book quotes Col. T. W. Higginson's description of the 'lonesome valley' as a term for spiritual searching among the singers.
verses:
My brudder, want to get religion?
Go down in de lonesome valley,
Go down in de lonesome valley, my Lord;
Go down in de lonesome valley,
To meet my Jesus dere.
O feed oh milk and honey.
O John he write de letter.
And Mary and Marta read 'em.

title: Not Weary Yet
origin: Slave Songs of the United States (1867), No. 16, page 12; Port Royal Islands, South Carolina, collected by C. P. Ware.
note: Source verified directly against the Internet Archive's full-text scan of the original 1867 edition.
verses:
O me no weary yet,
O me no weary yet,
I have a witness in my heart,
O me no weary yet.
Since I been in de field to fight.
I have a heaven to maintain.
De bond of faith are on my soul.
Ole Satan toss a ball at me.
Him tink de ball would hit my soul.
De ball for hell and I for heaven.

title: Go in the Wilderness
origin: Slave Songs of the United States (1867), No. 19, page 14; Port Royal Islands, South Carolina, collected by C. P. Ware.
note: Source verified directly against the Internet Archive's full-text scan of the original 1867 edition. The editors note its second section shares roots with the Methodist hymn 'Ain't I glad I got out of the wilderness.'
verses:
I wait upon de Lord,
I wait upon de Lord,
I wait upon de Lord, my God,
Who take away de sin of the world.

If you want to find Jesus, go in the wilderness,
Go in de wilderness, go in de wilderness,
Mournin' brudder, go in de wilderness,
I wait upon de Lord.
You want to be a Christian.
You want to get religion.
If you spec' to be converted.
O weepin' Mary.
